# Pāyāsi Sutta (DN 23 (PTS DN ii 316))
**ID:** DN 23 (PTS DN ii 316)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Pāyāsi Sutta
**PTS:** DN ii 316
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/dn23
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0102m.mul9.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pāyāsi Sutta* (DN 23) is the tenth and final discourse of the *Mahāvagga* of the *Dīghanikāya* [Nguyen Van Thuong]. Set in Setabyā in the Kosala country, it depicts an extended and lively debate between the Buddhist elder Kumāra Kassapa and Governor Pāyāsi [Winternitz 1933; Nguyen Van Thuong]. Pāyāsi champions a skeptical materialist viewpoint, asserting that there is no other world, no rebirth, and no retribution for deeds [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983; Nguyen Van Thuong]. To defend his thesis, Pāyāsi describes gruesome experiments conducted on dying criminals to observe whether an escaping soul or immaterial essence could be detected [Analayo 2018]. Kumāra Kassapa refutes his objections through a sequence of vivid parables—including tales of foolish and wise caravan leaders and a cheating dice player—which were preserved independently in the Pāli Jātaka collection (JA 1 and JA 91) without the later identification of the protagonists as the Bodhisatta [Analayo 2014; Appleton 2010; SuttaCentral]. Pāyāsi eventually takes refuge in the Triple Gem, and the discourse concludes with instructions on proper lay offerings (*dāna*) [Norman 1983; Gaffney 2003; Nguyen Van Thuong]. The text notably takes place after the parinibbāna of the Buddha; commentarial tradition in Dhammapāla's *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* states that the sutta was delivered after the distribution of the Buddha's relics and the erection of the commemorative thūpas [Norman 1983; Winternitz 1933].
The sutta is widely recognized for its philosophical dialogue form, compared by scholars to Platonic dialogues and the *Milindapañha* [Winternitz 1933]. Extensive parallels exist across traditions, including *Dīrgha-āgama* 7 (DĀ 7), *Madhyama-āgama* 71 (MĀ 71), Taishō 45, and the Jain second Uvaṅga, the *Rāyapaseṇaijja* [Frauwallner 1997; SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus strongly aligns the sutta with these Chinese counterparts (ZH_T01_0026, ZH_T01_0001, ZH_T01_0045) and records text reuse with Sanskrit and Tibetan Vinaya and Abhidharma works [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pāli canon, DharmaNexus identifies over 7,600 shared passages across 258 texts, with prominent formulaic matches in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 3, AN 8, AN 4), *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 42), and discourses of the *Majjhima Nikāya* (MN 93, MN 84, MN 41, MN 60) [DharmaNexus].

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral entry for dn23 (Pāyāsisutta) — Basic metadata, English title, summary blurb, and curated parallels (DĀ 7, MĀ 71, T 45, Ja 91, Mil 5.4.5).

- [Gaffney 2003] Sean D. Gaffney, The Jātakanidānakathā: A Critical Study (2003) — Citation of the Pāyāsi Sutta regarding the proper performance of lay dāna.
- [Norman 1983] K. R. Norman, Pali Literature, A History of Indian Literature Vol. VII (1983) — Account of the debate between Pāyāsi and Kassapa, Dhammapāla's commentary on the sutta's post-parinibbāna date, and the emphasis on lay dāna.
- [Nguyen Van Thuong] Bhikkhu T.M.T. Nguyen Van Thuong, Study of the Concept of Citta as Depicted in the Pali Tipitaka — Details of the sutta's position as the tenth sutta of the Mahāvagga, the setting in Setabyā, Pāyāsi's wrong views, and his conversion.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. II: Buddhist Literature and Jaina Literature (1933) — Characterization of the lively dialogue between Pāyāsi and Kumāra Kassapa, comparison to Platonic dialogues, and note of the Jain parallel.
